title: Prejudice & discrimination
examples: What is the difference between prejudice and discrimination?
How does social identity theory explain group behaviour?

explain.say: Today we will explore social identity theory in psychology. This theory helps us understand group behaviour. It suggests that part of our self-concept comes from the groups we belong to.

draw.text: Social Identity Theory: Self from Groups

explain.say: Our social identity means the part of who we are based on group membership. For example, being a student at this school is part of your identity. It gives us a sense of belonging.

draw.text: Belonging shapes who we think we are.

explain.say: The theory suggests we naturally favour our own group, the in-group. This tendency is called in-group bias. We tend to view our own group positively.

draw.text: In-group bias: Favouring your own group.

explain.say: Stereotypes are oversimplified beliefs about a group of people. These beliefs are often inaccurate and can lead to prejudice. They are generalizations, not facts.
Discrimination is the unfair action taken against someone because of group membership. It is the behaviour resulting from prejudice. For example, refusing service based on appearance.
In real life, think about team sports. You might cheer louder for your school team. This shows in-group favouritism in action. You feel connected to your team.

faq.q: What is the difference between prejudice and discrimination?
faq.a: Prejudice is a negative attitude or belief about a group. Discrimination is the unfair action taken towards a person because of their group membership. You might also ask, "What is the difference between thinking and acting?" or "Is prejudice just in your head?"
asks: What is the difference between prejudice and discrimination?
How are attitudes different from actions?

faq.q: Does social identity theory mean we only care about our own group?
faq.a: Not entirely. The theory explains that group membership is a major part of our self-concept. However, it also suggests we can develop empathy for other groups. You could also ask, "Can we overcome in-group bias?" or "Does belonging always cause bias?"
asks: Does social identity mean we ignore others?
Is it impossible to care about other groups?
How much does group membership affect us?

faq.a: Stereotypes are oversimplifications that ignore individual differences. They are mental shortcuts that can be inaccurate. You might also ask, "Are stereotypes always harmful?" or "Can stereotypes ever be true?"
asks: What is the basis of a stereotype?

faq.q: How does this theory explain conflict between groups?
faq.a: Conflict can arise when group identities are threatened or when resources are perceived as scarce. The need to maintain a positive social identity can drive competition. You could also ask, "Why do groups compete?" or "What causes intergroup conflict?"
asks: Why do groups fight over things?

faq.q: Is it possible to change our social identity?
faq.a: While our core identity is complex, exposure to different perspectives and challenging our assumptions can lead to change. Education and direct experience are powerful tools. You might also ask, "Can we learn to value other groups?" or "Is identity fixed?"
asks: Can I change how I see other groups?
What helps us change our views?

facts: Social identity theory suggests our self-concept includes group memberships.
In-group bias is the tendency to favour one's own group.
Stereotypes are oversimplified and generalized beliefs about groups.
Discrimination is the observable behaviour resulting from prejudice.

quiz.say: A student assumes all people from a certain region are good cooks.
quiz.why: This is an oversimplified belief about a whole group, which fits the definition of a stereotype.

wrong.1: Prejudice is the attitude, not the belief itself.
wrong.2: Discrimination requires an action, not just a thought.
wrong.3: Social identity is the source of the feeling, not the belief.

quiz.say: Showing favouritism towards your own sports team over another team.
quiz.why: This specific favouritism towards your own group is known as in-group bias.

wrong.0: Stereotyping is a general belief, while this is a specific favouritism.
wrong.1: This is an internal feeling, not an external action.
wrong.2: Self-concept is the whole idea of 'self', not just the bias.

quiz.say: When a person refuses to let another person enter a club because of their clothing style.
quiz.why: Refusing entry is a clear, observable action taken against someone, which is discrimination.

wrong.1: Prejudice is the thought; refusing entry is the action.
wrong.2: This action could happen even if the person isn't part of the immediate in-group.
wrong.3: Social identity is the theory; this is the behaviour.
